Tequila — U.S. Category Intelligence

Category structure, premium dynamics, channel composition, and competitive concentration · R12 trailing

Executive Summary

Tequila is the single most consequential category dynamic in U.S. beverage alcohol today. In the trailing 13 months, total tequila 9L volume grew +14.2%, against a U.S. spirits category that grew +2.1% overall — a 12-point spread that puts tequila on a clear trajectory to overtake American whiskey in 9L volume by the late 2020s at current rates.

The growth is structurally premium, not promotional. Revenue grew +22.4%, an 8.2-point price/mix premium that is the strongest of any major category. The premiumization is most acute in the prestige tier (+22%) and super-premium tier (+14%), while call tier declined -1.2% and well tier declined -5.4% — a clean tier-shift signal with no premium plateau yet visible.

The category is concentrated and concentrating further. The top 10 anonymized brands accounted for 71% of category 9L volume, with the top 3 alone capturing 38%. The innovation pipeline remains unusually productive — new items in the 0–12 month cohort grew at +44% velocity, well above the spirits-category average of +28% for that cohort.

Category Composition

Tequila divides into five primary sub-categories. Blanco remains the largest at 38% of volume with steady +18% growth — a mature core that continues to expand. Reposado at 26% of volume grew +14%. Añejo at 12% grew +11%. Mezcal at just 4% of volume grew +27%, the fastest sub-segment in the entire spirits category. The broader "other" segment (gold, mixto, and aged formats outside the three main styles) declined -8% as consumers migrate toward 100% agave designations.

Sub-category growth — R12 vs prior R12
Bar length indexes share of category 9L volume; color encodes R12 growth rate
The Cristalino phenomenon: The clear-aged style grew from approximately 2% of category volume three years ago to 6% today, with R12 growth of +31%. It is reshaping consumer expectations of what "premium" tequila looks like and is driving disproportionate revenue mix gains. We expect Cristalino to be tracked as a distinct sub-category in industry reporting within 24 months.

Premium Dynamics

The premiumization signature is one of the cleanest tier-shift patterns in current spirits data. The growth-by-tier pattern is monotonic — there is no "premium plateau" yet, no point at which consumer interest tapers off as price rises.

Tier growth — diverging from zero
Tequila R12 vs prior R12 by price tier · positive teal, negative coral

Tequila's premium index — revenue share divided by 9L share — stands at 132 (where 100 = category average), the highest of any major spirits category and well above the spirits average of 104. For every 1.0 unit of 9L share a tequila brand holds, it captures 1.32 units of revenue share — a structural margin position that no other category currently offers at scale.

The on-premise channel is leading premiumization within tequila. In fine dining and country club sub-channels, the tequila premium index reaches 155–165, meaning tequila over-indexes on revenue by 55–65% versus its volume share in those venues. Casino and hotel sub-channels are close behind at 118–128.

Channel & Sub-Channel Performance

The on-premise channel accounts for 38% of tequila volume — meaningfully higher than the spirits average of 33%. On-prem grew +18% in R12 while off-prem grew +12%, widening the channel spread. Tequila is increasingly an on-premise-led category despite still being volume-larger off-premise — a pattern that mirrors the early-2010s craft beer trajectory.

On-prem sub-channel growth — tequila category
Tequila category R12 growth by on-prem sub-channel

Tequila is becoming the second-most-poured spirit in casual dining (after vodka), reshaping cocktail program design across the sub-channel. The margarita has shifted from a single placeholder to a multi-tier price ladder — several casual dining chains now carry six or more tequila SKUs on the cocktail list, up from two or three a decade ago.

Competitive Landscape (Anonymized)

Category concentration has clear analytic implications. The top 10 brands capture 71% of volume, but the distribution within that 10 is steep — the top brand alone holds 14% of category volume, brands 2 and 3 combined hold 24%, and brands 4–10 hold 33%. The remaining 29% of volume is distributed across the long tail.

Brand concentration — anonymized share of tequila 9L volume
Top 10 brands account for 71% of category volume; top 3 alone account for 38%

Three patterns emerge in the brand-level data without identifying specific brands:

Concentration with mobility. While the top 10 list has been roughly stable in count over five years, the rank order within it has shifted significantly. Two of today's top 5 brands were outside the top 10 five years ago. The category rewards specific positioning more than legacy distribution.

Price-anchor effects. Brands priced at the boundary of two tiers — for example, near the $30 retail call/premium boundary — consistently outperform brands priced cleanly within a tier. The "tier-stretcher" position is the most productive in current data.

Sub-channel fragmentation. The top 5 brands account for 78% of casino tequila volume but only 64% of casual dining tequila volume. The category is more fragmented in mass on-premise — a meaningful read for any brand planning a casual-dining-led launch.

Strategic Implications

For Distributors
  • 1Tier-stretching is the highest-margin positioning. Brands priced at the boundary between two tiers are outgrowing both cleanly-tier-positioned brands. Portfolio decisions should explicitly weigh price-band coverage.
  • 2Casino and hotel are the highest-velocity placements. Focused chain-account programs in these sub-channels deliver stronger ROI than mass full-bar coverage for premium and above SKUs.
  • 3Cristalino warrants distinct tracking and reporting. The format is fundamentally reshaping category economics but is currently buried inside aggregated "aged" or "premium" categories in most distributor reports.
For Retailers
  • 1Over-allocate shelf space to premium and super-premium tequila. The tiers over-index on revenue at 1.5× their volume share — current planograms under-represent them in roughly 60% of audited accounts.
  • 2Cristalino and mezcal need dedicated facings, not adjacent buckets. The growth velocity and price-point sensitivity warrant separate treatment from aged tequila and blanco.
  • 3Margarita-adjacent assortment matters more than expected. Premium triple sec, fresh lime, and ice-quality at on-premise are implicit drivers of category expansion at restaurants and should be tracked as adjacent business.
For Suppliers
  • 1Innovation should target the call/premium boundary — the highest-mobility price band in the category and where two of the last five years' breakout brands first emerged.
  • 2Mezcal and Cristalino positioning require distinct go-to-market. Aggregated "agave portfolio" marketing under-resources both formats; they have non-overlapping consumer demographics.
  • 3On-premise sub-channel focus delivers higher premium index lift than off-premise expansion at the same investment level — a 1.55× index in country club placements versus 1.32 category average.

Premium tier — acceleration across U.S. spirits

Tier-level acceleration, category mix shifts, and sub-channel index dynamics · R12 trailing

Executive Summary

Premium-and-above tiers — premium, super-premium, and prestige — now represent 47% of U.S. spirits revenue, up from 38% five years ago. R12 growth stands at +12.4%, and acceleration (the change in growth rate from prior R3 to current R3) is +3.1pt — the highest acceleration reading since the post-pandemic premium boom of 2021.

The pattern is consistent with structural tier-shift, not promotional pull-forward. Volume growth at prestige is roughly half of revenue growth (volume +10.8%, revenue +18.4%) — a 7-point spread that indicates consumers are reaching for higher-priced bottles rather than buying more of the same.

The agave portfolio is doing disproportionate work. Tequila and mezcal together account for 53% of all spirits prestige-tier growth in R12 — meaning a single botanical family is now driving the majority of premium expansion across the entire category.

Tier-Level Acceleration

The acceleration pattern across tiers is monotonic. Acceleration is positive in prestige (+4.2pt), super-premium (+3.0pt), and premium (+1.1pt) — the three premium tiers. Call shows mild deceleration (-0.4pt) and well shows accelerated decline (-2.1pt). Every tier above premium is speeding up; every tier below premium is either stable or slowing.

Tier acceleration — R3 growth vs prior R3 growth
Acceleration measured as percentage-point change in growth rate; positive = accelerating, negative = decelerating
The acceleration is structural, not promotional. Premium volume growth is roughly half of premium revenue growth — consumers reaching for higher-priced bottles, not buying more of the same. This is a tier-mix shift, not a discount-pull effect.

Category-Level Premium Movements

Premium share — premium-and-above as a percent of category volume — varies widely across spirits categories. Tequila is the most premium-skewed at 67%, followed by whiskey at 58% and gin at 51%. Vodka and rum remain the most mass-tier-anchored.

Premium-and-above share by category
Bar shows premium-and-above as a % of category volume; trend annotation indicates 24-month premium-share change

Whiskey is the cautionary signal in this dataset. While whiskey has the second-most premium mix, its premium share has plateaued at 58% over the last 24 months — the premium shift in whiskey may have largely run its course. Tequila, by contrast, continues to add 2–3 points of premium share per year and shows no plateau yet.

Gin's relatively high premium mix is the structural story most under-covered in industry conversation. Craft gin and high-end botanical formats have shifted 13 points of category share into premium-and-above over the trailing 36 months, with no flattening yet visible.

Sub-Channel Premium Dynamics

The on-premise sub-channel mix is where the premium tier reaches its sharpest expression. Country club, fine dining, and airport sub-channels all show premium index values above 130 — meaning premium SKUs over-index on revenue by 30%+ versus their volume share in those venues.

Premium index by on-prem sub-channel
Premium index = revenue share ÷ 9L volume share, scaled so 100 = category average. Values above 100 indicate premium over-indexing

The two sub-channels below 1.0 — casual dining and sports/entertainment — are where premium SKUs under-index on revenue versus their volume placement. This is a function of consumer mindset by venue: in a sports bar or casual chain, beverage purchases skew to well and call tiers; in a country club or fine dining venue, the consumer expects and selects premium-and-above.

Strategic Implications

For Distributors
  • 1Prioritize prestige-tier programs. Prestige is accelerating fastest (+4.2pt) and carries the highest premium index. Distributor sales programs that index too heavily on premium and super-premium may be under-allocating the highest-mobility tier.
  • 2Agave portfolio breadth is a structural advantage. Distributors with broad tequila and mezcal portfolios are over-indexing on prestige-tier growth by 12–15 points versus distributors with narrow agave coverage.
  • 3Country-club and fine-dining sub-channel programs deliver the highest premium-index ROI. Sales effort directed at these venues yields ~1.5× more revenue per case than equivalent effort directed at casual dining.
For Retailers
  • 1Re-allocate shelf to premium-and-above. Premium-and-above commands 47% of revenue but typically 30–35% of facings in audited accounts — a structural mismatch that under-captures category revenue potential.
  • 2Prestige is now the marginal expansion opportunity. Five years ago this was super-premium; the consumer has moved up a tier, and most planograms have not yet followed.
  • 3Whiskey premium has plateaued. Whiskey premium shelf allocation should be held flat or modestly trimmed; the marginal facings should move to agave premium and prestige formats.
For Suppliers
  • 1Launch at prestige, not premium. Prestige is the highest-mobility entry point in current data. New brands launching at prestige reach breakout velocity at nearly double the rate of premium-tier launches.
  • 2The agave halo is real and portable. Non-agave brands launched within agave-adjacent portfolios are growing at +18% vs +11% for equivalent launches in non-agave portfolios.
  • 3Sub-channel-first launch sequencing outperforms. Brands that launch in country club and fine dining first, then expand to broader on-prem, show 2.1× higher 24-month velocity than brands that launch broad.

On-premise channel — performance and outlook

Sub-channel performance, on-prem vs off-prem asymmetries, and category mix within on-premise · R12 trailing

Executive Summary

The on-premise channel has fundamentally re-priced itself out of the pandemic recovery and into a structurally healthier position. R12 volume growth of +8.6% outpaced off-premise (+6.2%) for the first time since 2019. The channel now accounts for 33% of volume but 42% of revenue — a 9-point premium-mix spread that is wider than at any point in tracked history.

The recovery is uneven by tier and venue. Premium and prestige tiers in on-prem grew +14% to +18%, while well and call tiers declined -3% to -5% — a sharper tier-shift than off-prem's parallel pattern. Casino and hotel sub-channels are leading; casual dining lags meaningfully.

The implication for distributors and brands is that on-prem is no longer a recovery story; it is now the structural premium-mix anchor for the U.S. business. Investment patterns built on a post-pandemic assumption of weak on-prem demand are likely under-resourced for the current state of the channel.

Sub-Channel Performance

The eight on-prem sub-channels show meaningfully different trajectories. Casino at +15% growth is the fastest-growing, driven by gaming-industry recovery and premiumization of beverage program design. Hotel at +12% reflects business-travel normalization. Country club and fine dining at +9% are growing at near-identical rates with structurally different drivers.

On-prem sub-channel growth — R12 vs prior R12
R12 9L volume growth by on-prem sub-channel
Casino is the fastest-growing on-prem sub-channel at +15% volume. Three forces overlay: gaming-industry recovery, structural premiumization of beverage menus to match destination-resort positioning, and post-pandemic tourism returning above 2019 levels.

Casual dining's +3% growth deserves attention. This sub-channel represents roughly 28% of on-prem volume — the largest single sub-channel — but is growing at one-third the casino rate. The implication is that the on-prem recovery is concentrated in destination and premium venues; the mass-on-prem segment remains soft.

Channel Mix Compared

The structural differences between on-prem and off-prem are widening, not converging. On-prem is now meaningfully more premium-tier-concentrated and growing faster on both volume and revenue.

On-premise vs off-premise — key indicators
R12 comparison across volume growth, revenue growth, and premium index

The 36-point gap in premium index (127 vs 91) is the dataset's strongest single indicator that on-prem and off-prem are evolving as structurally different businesses, not parallel channels. Brand strategy that treats them as equivalent placement opportunities is likely under-performing in both.

Category Dynamics in On-Prem

The category mix within on-prem differs meaningfully from off-prem. Tequila is now the largest spirits category by on-prem 9L volume — a position it does not hold in off-prem. Wine, vodka, and whiskey trail at lower on-prem volume shares than their off-prem positions.

Category mix within on-prem — share and R12 growth
Bar shows category share of on-prem volume; growth annotation indicates R12 9L volume growth

Tequila's leadership position in on-prem is the most consequential cross-category dynamic in current data. The margarita has shifted from a single placeholder cocktail to a multi-tier price ladder. On-prem operators are routinely carrying 6+ tequila SKUs on the cocktail list — a structural change that has expanded the channel's appetite for premium agave SKUs.

Strategic Implications

For Distributors
  • 1Re-weight on-prem coverage toward destination venues. Casino, hotel, country club, and fine dining are where premium-tier growth concentrates. Distributor coverage models that allocate sales effort proportional to volume under-resource these sub-channels relative to their revenue contribution.
  • 2Casual dining requires a different go-to-market. The sub-channel's +3% growth signals that mass on-prem is in a different phase than destination on-prem; programs designed for high-velocity venues may not work in casual chains.
  • 3The cocktail-menu sell is the new shelf-set sell. Cocktail list placement is the on-prem equivalent of off-prem facing share; distributors with menu-design partnerships are pulling ahead.
For Suppliers
  • 1Launch sequence: destination on-prem first. Brands that establish in casino, hotel, country club, and fine dining before expanding to casual chains show 2.1× higher 24-month velocity than brands that launch broad.
  • 2Cocktail design support is now table stakes. Programs that provide on-prem operators with cocktail recipes, training, and menu design are showing 25–35% velocity premiums over equivalent brands without operator-facing programs.
  • 3Premium index, not volume, is the on-prem KPI. Brands optimizing for case volume in on-prem are leaving margin on the table; the channel's premium index of 127 means revenue captures structurally outsize the volume metric.

Innovation pipeline — what's working in new items

Cohort velocity, category hotspots, channel adoption sequencing, and breakout patterns · R12 view · 24-month launch window

Executive Summary

The U.S. wine and spirits innovation pipeline saw 1,847 new SKUs launched in the trailing 24 months. The 0–12 month cohort grew at +44% velocity in R12 — a 30+ point premium over established SKUs (cohort growth of +12% for 48+ month items). The differential is the highest in tracked history and signals consumer appetite for new entries is at a multi-year high.

The breakout rate — new items reaching +20% growth in their first 12 months — stands at 23%, up from 17% three years ago. The category producing the most productive innovation is tequila and mezcal (33% of launches, 41% of breakouts), followed by RTDs (24% of launches, 19% of breakouts) and whiskey (18% of launches, 14% of breakouts).

The structural finding most worth flagging: tier-stretchers — new items priced at the boundary between two tiers — represent 14% of launches but 23% of breakouts. The pattern suggests consumer trial is unlocked by perceived value at a specific price point, not by category novelty alone.

Maturity Cohort Analysis

The growth curve across maturity cohorts is the cleanest signal of innovation health in current data. The 0–12 month cohort is growing at +44%, the 12–24 month cohort at +28%, and growth decays smoothly through 36 months. The 48+ month cohort — established SKUs — grew at +2% in R12.

R12 growth by SKU maturity cohort
9L volume growth by months-since-launch maturity bucket

The decay rate from cohort to cohort is the structural read. A smooth decay (44 → 28 → 12 → 5 → 2) indicates that new items are gaining real placement and velocity, not just initial trial. A steep decay between the 0–12 and 12–24 month cohorts would signal that launches are bursting and fading — a pattern characteristic of unsustainable distribution pushes. The current decay shape suggests sustained consumer pull for new entries, not a launch-driven distribution bubble.

Category Hotspots for Innovation

Innovation is heavily concentrated in three categories: tequila and mezcal, RTDs, and whiskey. The interesting comparison is the launch-to-breakout ratio — which categories convert launches into outsized successes.

Innovation by category — share of launches vs share of breakouts
A category over-indexes when breakout share exceeds launch share; tequila/mezcal is the strongest over-indexer

Tequila and mezcal show 41% breakout share against 33% launch share — a meaningful over-index that suggests the category's launch productivity exceeds its launch volume. RTDs show the inverse pattern (24% of launches, 19% of breakouts), suggesting the category is over-launching relative to its absorption capacity. Whiskey shows a similar under-index at 18% / 14%.

The most productive launch positioning is now premium-and-above tequila or mezcal at a tier-stretching price point — a profile that yields a breakout probability of approximately 38% versus the category-blended average of 23%.

Channel Placement Velocity

How fast a new item reaches scale placement depends meaningfully on which on-prem sub-channel it enters first. The fastest-adopting sub-channels are casino, hotel, and fine dining; the slowest are casual dining and sports/entertainment.

Days to 100 buying accounts — by entry sub-channel
Median days for new items to reach 100 accounts; lower bars are faster adoption

The 4× spread between casino (58 days) and casual dining (248 days) is the channel-placement signal most worth absorbing. Suppliers planning launch sequencing should treat sub-channel entry order as a primary lever, not a secondary tactic — the difference between launching casino-first versus casual-dining-first is roughly six months of compounding velocity.

Strategic Implications

For Distributors
  • 1Carve dedicated new-item velocity-tracking from established-item performance. The 30+ point growth differential between cohorts means averaging them obscures both signals — established SKUs look healthier than they are, and new items look lower-priority than they should be.
  • 2Sub-channel entry sequencing is the highest-leverage placement decision. Distributors that pre-build casino, hotel, and fine-dining launch slates outpace category placement velocity by 2–3× over distributors who place broad-first.
  • 3Agave innovation pipeline disclosure is now a sales-team need. Distributor sales teams without visibility into upcoming agave launches are losing on-prem cocktail-menu placement battles to teams that can pre-pitch.
For Suppliers
  • 1Tier-stretching is the highest-probability launch position. 38% breakout probability for tequila/mezcal launches at tier-boundary price points is the strongest single launch-positioning signal in current data.
  • 2RTD launches need a higher selection bar. The category is over-launching relative to absorption — 19% breakout rate against 24% launch share. Brands launching another RTD into the current pipeline face headwinds that didn't exist 24 months ago.
  • 3Launch sequencing: casino → hotel → fine dining → broader on-prem → off-prem. The compounding velocity advantage of correct sequencing is roughly 2× a parallel launch into broad placement.

Whiskey — U.S. category intelligence

Sub-category composition, the premium plateau, channel patterns, and tequila substitution · R12 trailing

Executive Summary

Whiskey is the second-largest spirits category in the U.S. at 26% of 9L volume, but is now growing at the slowest pace of any major spirits category. R12 9L volume grew +2.4%, against a spirits-category average of +3.2% — the first time in seven years whiskey has growth below the category average.

The premium dynamics tell the more interesting story. Whiskey premium share has plateaued at 58% after rising approximately 14 points over the past decade. The premium index has dropped from 118 three years ago to 110 today — meaning the revenue-mix advantage whiskey has held over its volume share is structurally eroding.

The category is bifurcating. Premium and prestige tiers in bourbon, Irish, and rye continue to grow at +6% to +14%. But scotch and Canadian sub-categories are declining at -2% to -3%. The "whiskey is hot" narrative that has driven brand investment for a decade no longer applies uniformly — it applies to specific sub-categories.

Sub-Category Composition

Six primary sub-categories. Bourbon at 45% of whiskey volume continues to dominate but is growing more slowly than five years ago. Tennessee at 14% is the steadier growth engine. Scotch (15%) and Canadian (12%) are in structural decline. Irish at 10% remains the secondary growth story. Rye at 4% is the volatile high-growth tail.

Whiskey sub-category share and R12 growth
Bar shows sub-category share of whiskey 9L volume; growth annotation indicates R12 vs prior R12

Bourbon's slowdown is the most consequential dynamic in the dataset. The category that powered whiskey premiumization for two decades is now growing at +3% versus +8% to +12% five years ago. The consumer who drove the bourbon boom is aging into stable consumption; the next generation is reaching for tequila. This is the single clearest cross-category substitution pattern in current data.

Premium Dynamics — The Plateau

Premium share varies meaningfully by sub-category, and the trajectory of premium share is the diagnostic. Scotch at 72% premium is the most premium-skewed but the sub-category is contracting in volume. Bourbon at 58% premium has plateaued — the premium shift in bourbon may have largely run its course. Rye at 68% premium is the most interesting positioning in the category.

Premium-and-above share by whiskey sub-category
Bar shows premium-and-above as a % of sub-category volume
Whiskey premium share has plateaued at 58% after rising 14 points over a decade. The era of structural whiskey premiumization is largely over; the next phase is sub-category-specific. Rye and Irish have room to run; bourbon and Tennessee likely do not.

Rye at 68% premium share is the most interesting positioning in the category. The sub-category is small (4% of whiskey volume) but is the most premium-anchored growth sub-category in whiskey. Brands launching at rye prestige show breakout rates approximately 1.4× the whiskey average — the most productive launch position currently identifiable within the category.

Channel & Consumption Patterns

Whiskey is the most off-premise-skewed major spirits category at 72% off-prem volume share, against a spirits-category average of 67%. The dynamic reflects consumption occasions — whiskey is disproportionately a home-consumption category, particularly for bourbon and scotch.

Channel structure — whiskey vs spirits average
Volume share and premium index by channel

In on-prem, the sub-channel distribution differs from tequila's. Whiskey indexes strongest in full-bar and fine-dining venues, where neat-and-rocks pours are the dominant serve. The category under-indexes in casino and hotel sub-channels relative to its overall volume share — a pattern consistent with whiskey's positioning as a contemplative rather than celebratory pour.

Strategic Implications

For Distributors
  • 1Rationalize scotch and Canadian SKU counts. Both sub-categories are declining and the marginal shelf is more productive with bourbon premium or tequila across nearly every account class.
  • 2Prioritize rye prestige programs. Rye is the highest-mobility positioning within whiskey, with launch breakout rates 1.4× the category average and premium index above 140.
  • 3Treat whiskey and tequila as substitutes, not adjacencies. Bourbon's slowdown correlates negatively with tequila's acceleration in nearly every region — the same consumer is making the switch.
For Retailers
  • 1Reallocate whiskey shelf toward premium bourbon and Irish. Aged-statement bourbons (10yr+) command 25–30% revenue premium; over-allocate space within bourbon premium.
  • 2Scotch and Canadian facings should be modestly trimmed. Both sub-categories show declining volume and flat premium mix — the strategic justification for current shelf allocation has weakened.
  • 3Rye warrants dedicated facings, not adjacent bourbon placement. The growth profile and consumer demographic warrant separate treatment within the whiskey set.
For Suppliers
  • 1Bourbon launches face structural headwinds. Innovation should focus on aged statements, single barrel, and small-batch positioning — not new mass-tier entries.
  • 2Rye is the highest-leverage launch position within whiskey. Small base, fast growth, premium-skewed consumer — the structural conditions for breakout brand emergence.
  • 3Irish whiskey premiumization is under-explored. The sub-category is growing and premium-shift has room to run; current premium share at 60% is well below scotch's 72% ceiling.

Hoodie Intelligence Brief

Rum — U.S. category intelligence

Sub-category dynamics, the premium aged opportunity, channel asymmetries, and the structural decline · R12 trailing

Executive Summary

Rum is the only major U.S. spirits category in structural decline. R12 9L volume contracted -2.8% while the broader spirits category grew +3.2% — a 6-point underperformance gap that has widened in each of the last four years. Revenue declined -1.2%, somewhat softening the volume contraction through limited premiumization but not enough to reverse the trajectory.

The category's premium index of 85 (where 100 = category average) is the lowest of any major spirits category, meaning rum under-indexes on revenue versus its volume share by 15%. This is the structural problem the category faces: consumer interest in rum is concentrated in the value tier where margin is thinnest.

The single bright spot is premium aged rum. The sub-segment grew +13.4% in R12 — the only meaningful growth driver in the category. But it represents only 6% of category volume and is unlikely to offset the larger declines in light, spiced, and flavored rum at current trajectories.

Sub-Category Dynamics

The sub-category-level data exposes the category's challenge. Light rum and coconut/flavored rum together account for 52% of category volume and are declining at -4% and -8% respectively. These two sub-categories alone explain most of the category's underperformance.

Rum sub-category share and R12 growth
Bar shows sub-category share of rum 9L volume; growth annotation indicates R12 vs prior R12
The consumer who drove rum consumption a decade ago — younger drinkers favoring sweet, mixed-drink occasions — has shifted decisively toward tequila and seltzer-RTD formats. Light rum's -4% decline correlates directly with tequila's +18% acceleration in the same demographic.

Premium aged and craft (rhum agricole, single estate) together represent only 10% of category volume but are growing at +13% to +21%. The growth is real but the base is too small to drive category-level reversal. For the category to return to flat growth, premium aged would need to roughly triple in share over the next 36 months — possible but unlikely at current pacing.

The Premium Aged Opportunity

Premium aged rum is the only growth narrative the category currently supports. The sub-segment includes 8-year and older aged formats, single estate / cask-strength offerings, and Caribbean origin-specified rums. Growth of +13.4% in R12 makes it competitive with mid-tier tequila growth — but the category-level visibility is far lower.

Premium-and-above share by rum sub-category
Bar shows premium-and-above as a % of sub-category volume

Caribbean tourism recovery above 2019 levels has been the single largest demand-side driver of premium aged rum growth. Consumers returning from Caribbean travel are seeking aged rum at retail, mirroring the agave tourism dynamic that drove tequila adoption in the late 2010s. The structural conditions for a "rum moment" exist — but only in premium aged, and only at scale that would require a brand-led narrative the category currently lacks.

Channel & Consumption

Rum's channel split mirrors the spirits average roughly evenly. The interesting divergence is in premium index by channel: rum's on-prem premium index of 112 is meaningfully higher than its off-prem premium index of 78. This is because premium aged rum sells in cocktail-focused on-prem venues, while value-tier light and spiced rum dominate off-prem.

Rum channel structure
Volume share and premium index by channel

The path to category recovery, if one exists, runs through the on-prem channel. The on-prem channel is the only realistic trial pathway for premium aged rum at scale. Cocktail-driven consumer trials of mai tai, dark and stormy, and daiquiri rebuilds provide the demonstration occasions that off-prem consumer marketing has been unable to deliver alone.

Strategic Implications

For Distributors
  • 1Rum SKU rationalization is overdue. Light and flavored sub-categories should consolidate to top-velocity SKUs; the long tail no longer earns its shelf space.
  • 2Premium aged rum deserves dedicated sales coverage. The on-prem opportunity is where the only meaningful growth lives; distributor sales effort proportional to category share under-resources it.
  • 3The on-prem channel is the only realistic recovery path. Off-prem rum is a managed-decline business; distributors that build cocktail-driven on-prem programs in destination venues can grow share even as the category contracts.
For Retailers
  • 1Contract rum shelf space in absolute terms. The marginal facings should reallocate to tequila premium where the demonstrated consumer-volume substitution is concentrated.
  • 2Premium aged should be over-represented within remaining rum allocation. The 6% category share warrants closer to 15–20% of facings given growth velocity and margin contribution.
  • 3Coconut and flavored rum facings should be substantially reduced. The category is in -8% decline with no visible inflection signal.
For Suppliers
  • 1Light rum launches face structural headwinds. Innovation should target premium aged exclusively; new mass-tier launches enter a contracting consumer base.
  • 2The cocktail-creation angle is the only on-prem trial pathway. Mai tai, dark and stormy, and daiquiri programs in destination on-prem venues are where consumer trial gets rebuilt.
  • 3Caribbean tourism partnerships and rum-distillery brand storytelling are the most productive marketing positions; the agave model of "tourism drives premium category adoption" applies directly.

Off-prem is chain-country: Warehouse club, mass merchant, online, and liquor chain derive 70%+ of their volume from A-class accounts — a small number of corporate buyers control nearly all the shelf decisions. Liquor independent is the inverse — fragmented across 75,000+ stores with no single account holding meaningful share. The right go-to-market is structurally different: chain-HQ programs for the concentrated channels, distributor case-rate programs for independent.
New item adoption velocity · median days to 100 accounts by sub-channel
Innovation receptivity bifurcates sharply: Warehouse club and mass merchant adopt new items in roughly 2–5 weeks — chain authorization is binary and decisive. Online DTC and large-format liquor chain follow at 2–3 months. Independent liquor and convenience take 5–7 months. The launch sequence is therefore chain-led — chain authorization builds broad placement quickly; independents follow once velocity is proven and the distributor sales force can carry the story.

Key insights · format-level patterns
Online / DTC · 28% format growth · 18d rollout velocity
The fastest-growing chain format in the dataset, with the fastest median rollout velocity of any format other than warehouse club. Premium-tier skew (format premium index 165). Implication for chain-team launch sequencing: this is the format-level beachhead for prestige launches — proof in this format unlocks the next wave.
Warehouse club · 14% format growth · deep volume concentration
High volume, high velocity per door, premium-skewed mix, fastest new-item rollout. The format with the highest expected return per authorization decision — every category line review is a major leverage moment for the chain teams that work this format.
Mass merchant · 9% format growth · value-tier skew
High volume but premium index 82 — structurally a value-tier format. Format-level implication: launches should be sequenced by tier fit, not by chain relationship strength. Premium launches don't belong here; value launches move fastest here.
Premium grocery · 8% format growth · premium index 124
Premium-tier mix on a high-volume base. The format that converts trade-up consumer behavior into volume most efficiently. Chain-team implication: this is the format to push premium SKU breadth — the buyer is shopping the format for premiumization.
Convenience · -2% format growth · premium index 62
The structural decliner. Value-tier consumer entrenchment, slowest rollout velocity, declining R12. Format-level implication: defend existing distribution; do not invest distributor effort in growth here.
Top 10 chain operators · ~33% of total chain volume
Chain concentration in the off-prem channel is structural. A small number of chain operators drive a disproportionate share of any given category's volume. The chain team is the customer that organizes commercial effort around this reality — and the platform structures its outputs to match.

Headroom Pareto · realized vs achievable cumulative volume share
How to read it: X-axis is account rank in the full segment universe (1 = highest-expected account, regardless of whether currently purchasing). Y-axis is cumulative volume as % of total addressable. The dashed teal line is the achievable cumulative — each account in the universe contributes its expected per-segment value to this line. The solid navy line is the realized cumulative — only purchasing accounts contribute their actual value; non-purchasing accounts add zero. The achievable line keeps climbing as more accounts enter the rank window; the realized line plateaus where the purchasing population thins out. The widening band between the two is the structural headroom — distribution gap plus velocity gap plus the multiplicative residual.
Headroom decomposition · where the gap actually lives
Choosing the lever: Distribution gap is the "add accounts" lever — accounts in the segment universe that aren't depleting at all. Velocity gap is the "lift what you have" lever — accounts currently depleting but below the top-quartile benchmark for their segment celli. Combined gap is the highest-leverage targets — accounts not yet depleting in segment cells with high achievable velocity. The three numbers add to the total headroom and direct the commercial workflow toward the right action.
Headroom by sub-segment · ranked by gap size
The working list: When the filter is set to "all" sub-channels, this table breaks the headroom down by sub-channel — telling chain teams, on-prem teams, and field commercial which sub-channels carry the most headroom in the current cut. When the filter is set to a specific sub-channel, the breakdown drills into account class within that sub-channel — A/B/C/D distribution of where the gap actually lives.
Methodology: For each segment cell, defined as the intersection of sub-channel × account class × census division, total addressable volume (TAMi) is computed as segment universe size × expected per-account value, where the expected per-account value is the top-quartile (P75i) observed depletion velocity for accounts within that cell. The achievable line on the chart is the cumulative sum of expected values across every account in the universe — purchasing or not. The realized line is the cumulative sum of actual depletions, where non-purchasing accounts contribute zero. The total headroom thus captures both the distribution gap (accounts not yet purchasing) and the velocity gap (purchasing accounts below the segment benchmark), with the multiplicative residual surfaced separately. All cells reflect N ≥ 10 accounts; cells below that threshold are pooled to the parent segment to preserve anonymization.
Connect a source
Hoodie gets sharper with more sources, not fewer. Connect your CRM, ERP, planning, communication, and BI systems, and the platform aligns each to the same anonymized analytical structure as the syndicated depletion data — your access controls preserved, the N≥10 minimum enforced on every shared cell.

≡Derived metrics framework✎⚙
Five analytical lenses derived from base measurements — POD, accounts sold, 9L volume, revenue
VELOCITY
9L ÷ Accounts Sold
Depth per buying account. Reads volume independent of distribution footprint — higher value means each transacting account is pulling more cases.
ACTIVATION RATE
Accounts Sold ÷ POD
Share of the carrying base that actually transacts in a given period. A category can have wide distribution that is mostly dormant — activation rate exposes that.
PREMIUM INDEX
Revenue Share ÷ 9L Share
Above 1.0 = category earns more revenue share than volume share (premium-skewed). Below 1.0 = category earns less revenue share than volume share (value-skewed).
PRICE/MIX GROWTH
Revenue Growth − 9L Growth
Positive value means revenue is growing faster than volume — the category is premiumizing or mix is improving. Negative signals deflation or mix degradation.
POD EFFICIENCY
9L Share ÷ POD Share
Volume produced per unit of distribution footprint. Above 1.0 = narrow-deep (concentrated volume in fewer accounts). Below 1.0 = wide-shallow (volume spread thin across many placements).
Direction: positive / premium-skewed / narrow-deep negative / value-skewed / wide-shallow
Methodology: Derived metrics are computed from observed Hoodie depletion data using transparent formulas documented per metric. Each metric falls into one of five families: distribution, velocity, mix, growth, or concentration. Computational formulas, source fields, and refresh cadence are documented inline per metric.

≡Cohort migration — what they brought, what they left behind✎⚙
Birth-year cohort tracking from consumer panel data · the categories each cohort added to their basket and the categories they abandoned as they aged forward five years
Methodology. Cohort tracking is built on consumer panel data with single-year-of-age recorded per panelist. Cohorts are defined by birth year, not age range — anyone born 1990-1999 is the same set of people in 2020 and 2025, simply five years older. Panel attrition is reweighted using standard projection methodology so that the tracked cohort remains representative across the window. The age ranges shown below are the cohort's current age, not a bucket boundary.

The 1980–89 cohort accelerated this trade-up trajectory — premium aged 12yr+ became their fastest-adding category as they aged into peak-earning years. For distributors, this is forward-looking pipeline intelligence: today's 21-25 year olds (born 2000–2004) will follow a comparable trajectory in the next five years.

What the table tells distributors. Buyer economics turns category strategy from a volume question into a lifetime-value question. Wine's 14.6-year tenure × 12.4 purchases × $387 produces roughly $70,000 in cumulative buyer spend — by far the highest lifetime value in beverage alcohol. Among spirits, Premium aged whiskey 15yr+ produces ~$21,000 in lifetime value through high annual spend ($584) sustained over a long tenure (11.2 years). At the other end, RTDs at 2.4-year tenure and 41% repeat produce ~$2,300 in lifetime value — fundamentally a churn-driven business where sustained growth requires constant new-buyer acquisition rather than retention. Single Malt's 84% repeat rate combined with $524 annual spend makes it the highest-retention spirits category in the panel data. Investment decisions across innovation, account targeting, and supplier conversations should reflect these structural differences.

Key insights
Demographic signals that shape placement strategy, supplier QBR positioning, and innovation evaluation — the analytical layer not present in standard syndicated depletion data
Key insight
Bourbon's primary buyer is 41–65 male.
70% of bourbon volume comes from buyers over 41, and 62% from male buyers. Category growth in the past decade has been driven by existing buyers trading up to premium SKUs rather than by new younger cohorts entering the category. For distributors, this shapes premium-aged placement strategy (existing-buyer accounts are the primary growth lever) and informs how to evaluate younger-focused bourbon launches against the category's historical growth pattern.
Key insight
Cristalino is 71% female — the most female-skewed sub-category in tequila.
Cristalino's 2.4:1 female-to-male ratio is among the highest in spirits overall. For distributors, this is direct placement intelligence — cristalino activation pays off most where the female premium buyer actually shops and dines, which informs both on-premise sub-channel targeting (luxury hotel, country club, fine dining over sports bar / steakhouse) and off-premise shelf positioning relative to other premium tequila.
Key insight
Premium Scotch demographics have been remarkably stable for a decade.
Premium Scotch is 72% male and 75% over age 45 — and those proportions haven't meaningfully shifted in ten years. The category isn't broadening; it's deepening within the same cohort. For distributors, this means premium scotch growth strategy is fundamentally different from category-expanding sub-categories: existing-buyer trade-up matters more than new-buyer acquisition, and account placement should follow where the 45+ male buyer already drinks.
Key insight
RTDs are demographically the youngest category — by a 17-point margin.
45% of RTD buyers are 21–30, versus 28% for vodka (the next-youngest category). The cohort is also aging with the category at +2 years over the past 3 years, meaning sustained RTD growth depends on engaging new younger cohorts rather than retaining existing buyers. For distributors, this affects both account targeting (which on-prem sub-channels actually reach the 21–30 demographic) and innovation evaluation (which RTD launches credibly recruit new buyers versus which ones repackage the existing audience).
Key insight
Wine is the most demographically balanced category in beverage alcohol.
Wine distributes nearly evenly across age brackets (12% / 20% / 24% / 28% / 16% from youngest to oldest) and across gender (49% female, 51% male). For distributors, this means wine portfolio strategy benefits from broad demographic coverage rather than narrow targeting — any single-demographic positioning typically addresses a quarter of the category at most, so distribution and account-targeting decisions should reflect the breadth of the buyer base.
How distributors use this view. Demographic intelligence at this granularity is not available in standard syndicated depletion reporting. Distributors gain three categories of leverage: supplier QBR conversations grounded in actual buyer composition rather than stated target audiences; sharper account-targeting decisions tied to who actually shops or dines where; and better innovation evaluation when new launches can be tested against the demographics of the sub-category they are entering. This is the analytical layer that turns category data into placement strategy.
Methodology: Demographic placement gap surfaces opportunities where a category index is high in a demographic segment but distribution is under-developed in census divisions populated by that demographic. Demographic indices are from Census ACS data joined to ZIP-level Hoodie depletions. Indices > 110 indicate over-index; < 90 under-index. All cells reflect N ≥ 100 panel households.

Data trust

How Hoodie Intelligence protects your data

Hoodie Intelligence operates as a data fiduciary to its distributor partners. Every output in the platform is governed by anonymization rules that make it structurally impossible to reverse-engineer specific brand performance, account identity, or wholesaler-specific positioning from the aggregated views.

This is the same trust architecture that has governed Hoodie since its inception. What's new is that the architecture is now visible, auditable, and enforced at the display layer — not just at the source.

Protected layers

What is never shown — anywhere, ever

  • ✕Brand names. No view, no chart, no AI brief identifies a specific brand. Tequila category data is presented as anonymized clusters (A, B, C…) where each cluster represents a brand family.
  • ✕Specific account names or addresses. Account-level identifiers never appear in any output. Account classification (A/B/C/D) is the most granular account dimension exposed.
  • ✕Single-wholesaler identifying data. No view exposes data that could identify a single contributing wholesaler within an aggregated market view. The "Wholesaler vs Industry" comparison shows your aggregated book against an aggregated industry composite — never against any single peer.
  • ✕Individual SKU performance below aggregation thresholds. SKU-level data is only exposed within aggregated groups (e.g., maturity cohorts, category, tier). No single SKU's specific performance is ever singled out by name.
  • ✕Account classes below N≥10. Account class breakdowns (A/B/C/D) are only rendered for cells with at least 10 underlying accounts. Cells below threshold are aggregated upward or omitted.
  • ✕Time-stamped specific events. No view exposes single transactions, single days, or single pricing actions. The most granular time period is monthly aggregate.
Aggregation rules

What is shown — the dimensions you can analyze

  • ✓Categories — Whiskey, Vodka, Tequila, Rum, Wine, and other major spirits and wine categories
  • ✓Sub-categories — Bourbon, Scotch, Blanco, Reposado, Mezcal, and ~30 other industry-standard sub-classifications
  • ✓Channels and sub-channels — On-premise (8 sub-channels) and off-premise (8 sub-channels)
  • ✓Price tiers — Prestige, Super-Premium, Premium, Call, Well
  • ✓Account classes — A (top-volume), B, C, D (long tail) — only with N≥10 accounts
  • ✓Census divisions — 9 standard U.S. census divisions plus state-level rollups where licensing permits
  • ✓Time periods — R3, R12, CYTD, period-over-period; 24-month rolling history
  • ✓Derived metrics — Velocity, premium index, POD efficiency, activation rate, acceleration
Anonymization flow

How distributor data becomes intelligence

Step 1Distributor depletion data
→
Step 2Aggregation engine — rolls up to category, sub-category, sub-channel, tier, account class
→
Step 3Anonymization rules — strip brand, strip account ID, apply N≥10 thresholds, cluster-shuffle
→
Step 4Display layer — every view, every chart, every AI brief

Each layer is enforced independently. A brand name cannot reach Step 4 even if Step 2 or Step 3 fails to strip it — the display layer itself enforces the constraint.

Cluster rotation

Why "Cluster A" is not consistent across views

In the Anonymous Position views, clusters labeled A, B, C are rotated independently for each view. The cluster labeled "A" in the on-premise backbar visualization is not the same brand as the cluster labeled "A" in the off-premise shelf visualization, or in any other cluster-labeled chart.

This is intentional — even if someone learns one cluster identity through external means (e.g., guessing that "Cluster J in Premium Tequila" is a specific brand based on growth profile), they cannot extrapolate that knowledge to other views. Cluster identity is per-view, not per-platform.

The structural protection: Even with perfect knowledge of one cluster's brand identity in one view, an observer cannot deduce a brand's identity in any other view. The same brand will be Cluster J in one chart, Cluster M in another, and Cluster D in a third.
Commitments

What Hoodie Intelligence will never do

  • ✕Sell or share raw depletion data with third parties
  • ✕Allow brand-level resolution of any aggregated view, including through any combination of views
  • ✕Provide outputs that violate WSWA member privacy or competitive position
  • ✕Change anonymization rules without WSWA Data Committee approval
  • ✕Permit AI-driven outputs that exceed the same anonymization constraints as direct queries
Reviewed by the WSWA Data Committee. Anonymization rules and platform output policies are subject to quarterly review by the Data Committee. Distributors hold veto rights on changes to anonymization rules (see Governance).
Governance

Who decides where this platform goes

Hoodie is owned by WSWA, a 100% distributor-member organization. Hoodie Intelligence operates as the licensed analytics and dashboarding partner, providing visualization, AI synthesis, and product engineering on top of the SipSource depletion dataset.

The practical implication: distributors who participate in SipSource are also the owner-operators of this platform. Hoodie Intelligence is an extension of distributor-owned infrastructure, not a vendor selling into it.

This is step one, not a VIP replacement. Hoodie Intelligence extends SipSource with modern dashboarding, AI synthesis, and analytical tooling. VIP continues as a separate operational data services partner. The platform stack expands — it does not replace existing relationships.
The Data Committee

Governing body — composition and authority

The WSWA Data Committee is the governing body for all product, data, and policy decisions on the platform. Composition and voting structure are designed to keep distributor authority structurally dominant.

Voting composition
7Distributor seats — rotated among WSWA member distributors with weighted representation across distributor size tiers
2WSWA leadership seats — institutional continuity and member advocacy
1Hoodie Intelligence operational seat — non-voting, advisory only; cannot block or pass measures
Decision thresholds

Quorum: 6 of 9 voting seats present

Majority: 5 of 9 voting seats in agreement

Distributor veto: Any 3 distributor seats can block changes to anonymization rules, data-sharing terms, or partner additions — regardless of overall majority

The veto right is the structural protection: even if WSWA leadership and the operational seat align on a change, distributors retain blocking authority on the dimensions that matter most.

Decision scope

What the Data Committee decides

  • ✓Product roadmap priorities — quarterly review of feature backlog and prioritization
  • ✓Anonymization rule changes — distributor-veto-protected; no changes without committee approval
  • ✓New data partner approvals — vetting and approval of any third-party data integrations (e.g., off-premise scanner, on-premise POS feeds)
  • ✓Output policy changes — what gets shown, what doesn't, at what aggregation thresholds
  • ✓Strategic partnerships and integrations — alliance decisions with suppliers, retailers, and adjacent platforms
  • ✓Annual strategic plan — review and approval of operating direction and platform expansion
Operating cadence

How the committee works

Quarterly
Roadmap review, prioritization, partner approvals, anonymization audit, output policy review
Monthly
Operational metrics review, product status updates, escalation handling
Ad-hoc
Policy or anonymization changes require 30-day notice and committee vote; emergency security or compliance issues may be handled within 72 hours with distributor coalition consent
Annual
Strategic plan approval, charter review, governance structure review, committee seat rotation
Why this structure

Owner-operators, not customers

Distributors are not customers of this platform. Distributors are owner-operators of an analytic capability that they collectively built (through Hoodie contributions to WSWA) and continue to govern (through the Data Committee).

Hoodie Intelligence operates the platform. Distributors decide where it goes.

This is the structural distinction from any vendor relationship: the people who contribute the data are the same people who decide how the data gets used. No vendor — including Hoodie Intelligence — has unilateral authority to change the terms.

What this means in practice. If a distributor coalition objects to a proposed feature, data partner, anonymization change, or output policy, that proposal does not move forward. The committee is not advisory — it is binding. Hoodie Intelligence operates inside the constraints the committee sets.

About the data — Hoodie®

data source · methodology · coverage

What it is: SipSource® is the wine and spirits industry's syndicated depletion data platform, owned by the Wine & Spirits Wholesalers of America (WSWA) and built from primary-source transactions between WSWA-member distributors and their retail accounts. Data is harmonized by Vermont Information Processing (VIP) from distributors' proprietary product and account taxonomies into a single standardized aggregation.

Coverage and scope: Hoodie represents approximately 70% of wholesale wine and spirits products by volume across all 50 states. The dataset includes more than 225,000 wine and spirits products and more than 450,000 on- and off-premise retail outlets. Data is sourced exclusively from WSWA-member distributors and is not shared or sold to third-party providers.

Period framework: Hoodie reports on a rolling 12-month basis (R12). The primary period comparison is R12 vs prior R12. Trend reads — what most analysts call "acceleration" — are calculated as the change between consecutive R12 growth rates.

Primary metrics:

  • Growth = (current 12mo volume − prior 12mo volume) ÷ prior 12mo volume × 100
  • Trend = current month's R12 growth − previous month's R12 growth (i.e., acceleration)
  • Share = 12mo volume of an item ÷ 12mo volume of the section total × 100
  • Share Change = current year's 12mo share − prior year's 12mo share

Dimensions tracked: Product Type · Product Class · Product Segment · Price Tier · Country of Origin · Domestic/Import · Package Type · Package Size · Region · Sub-Region · Appellation · On- vs Off-Premise · Chain/Independent · National/Regional account.

Forecasting: Hoodie Forecasting is built on machine-learning models that combine distributor depletions with macroeconomic indicators (inflation, unemployment, consumer confidence). Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) is published as 1–5% — the industry benchmark for depletion-forecast accuracy.

Subscription tiers: Forecasting · Silver · Gold · Platinum. Access progresses from quarterly reports and monthly newsletters at the entry levels to full online iDig access across both wine and spirits at Platinum.

Customer use cases: The dashboard renders Hoodie data through the lens of category, channel, sub-channel, and tier. Anonymization rules prohibit identifying specific brands, accounts, or wholesalers — all output is aggregated or clustered into anonymous groupings. Every view in this suite is built on these primitives: depletion volume, revenue, points of distribution, and accounts sold.
