Home — Daily intelligence

personalized landing · 20 daily reports

What it shows: The daily intelligence landing page. Personalized navy header at the top shows your wholesaler's R12 snapshot — 9L growth, revenue growth, premium index, R3 acceleration — with quick-status callouts for "Working in your book" and "Watching closely." Below the banner, a 20-card grid of daily reports framed against the wholesaler's book.

How to read it: Each card is a focused single-dimension report — top growers, top decliners, acceleration alerts, vs-industry gaps, sub-channel performance, supplier-QBR leverage, etc. Cards with the "•" symbol indicate the card has an override time period that differs from the global filter. The full grid follows a narrative arc: performance → competitive position → channels → tier mix → geography → strategy → composition.

Controls: Search bar at top filters visible cards. Global period selector applies a default R12, CYTD, R3, or CM frame across cards that don't override. View-status banner shows whether the current view matches the saved default or has been modified.

Customer use cases: Monday morning intelligence briefing. Where am I accelerating or slipping vs the industry composite? What is my premium-index leverage by category for supplier QBR conversations? Which sub-channels are hot? Where is my portfolio over- or under-concentrated? The full set of daily questions distributors normally answer through ad-hoc spreadsheet work, surfaced as standing reports.

Hoodie Intelligence ✨

AI analytical briefs · personalized + industry

What it shows: Claude-style search interface for on-demand analytical briefs. Six pre-canned industry briefs (tequila, whiskey, rum, premium tier dynamics, on-premise channel, innovation) plus a personalized "Your Q4 Performance Brief" generated from the wholesaler's own depletion data. Each brief contains executive summary, charted data, strategic implications, and supplier-QBR talking points.

How to read it: Click any suggestion pill or type a query into the search bar — the platform routes to the closest available brief via keyword inference. The featured navy pill is the personalized brief; the six bordered pills are industry briefs. Each brief renders in approximately 1.6 seconds with the same anonymization rules applied as the rest of the platform. Briefs can be downloaded as PDF for use in supplier meetings.

Controls: Search input for free-form queries. Suggestion pills for quick access. "← Ask another question" button returns to the landing page. "Download as PDF" exports the active brief via the browser print pipeline.

Customer use cases: Pre-meeting briefing prep. Supplier QBR document generation. Strategic context for board updates or commercial reviews. The personalized brief specifically supports Monday-morning planning by generating a tailored read of the wholesaler's book in seconds — the same exercise that traditionally requires hours of analyst time.

Build

The self-serve analytics surface — build any view, design it, and push it to a supplier deck

Report builder ✨

drag-and-drop analytics · 21 chart types · full visual design

What it is: A full drag-and-drop analytics surface modeled on the Tableau / Power BI workflow, running directly on Hoodie depletion data. Drag dimensions and measures onto the Rows, Columns, Filters, and Values shelves to compose any view; the chart and underlying table rebuild live. The shelves collapse to a one-line summary to reclaim chart space.

Chart types: 21 visualization types — table, cross-tab, bar, horizontal bar, stacked bar, line, area, combo, scatter, pie, donut, heatmap, KPI cards, box plot, bullet, waterfall, funnel, and more. The Show Me panel recommends valid chart types for the current field selection.

Calculated fields & parameters: Build custom measures with an Excel-style formula engine (IF / IFS / AND / OR / MIN / MAX, arithmetic, and table calcs such as running total, % of total, rank, moving average, difference from prior). Parameters are reusable what-if controls (number, integer, string, boolean, or date; free, list, or range-bound) that flow into calculated fields, reference lines, and measure swaps — change one control and every dependent view updates live.

Conditional formatting: Per-measure cell formatting in two modes — automatic color scales (red-green diverging, heatmap, in-cell bars) and Excel-style highlight rules (greater than, between, is negative, equals, etc.) with custom colors and automatic readable text contrast.

The Marks card — full visual design: Everything you can design in Tableau's Marks card. Shape (circle, square, triangle, diamond, plus, ring) and size for scatter and line marks; color as a single custom color, a palette, or encoded — color by a dimension gives each value a distinct color with a categorical legend, and color by a measure applies a continuous light-to-dark ramp with a gradient legend; mark opacity; and data labels showing value, % of total, or both, with adjustable decimals, placement (auto / outside / inside / center), and font size. Line and combo charts support dual-axis synchronization onto one shared scale.

Reference lines & forecasting: Add fixed or parameter-bound reference lines, linear or quadratic trend lines, and an N-period forecast with a confidence band on time-series charts.

Output: Each build is a Sheet (multiple sheets per workspace). Pin to dashboard sends a live tile to My / Team dashboard; Save report stores the full configuration to reopen and edit; Export produces image, data (CSV), or a slide for PPTX Studio. The natural-language bar ("Show me tequila headroom by sub-channel in R12") composes a build for you.

Anonymization: Every cut respects the Hoodie rules — category, sub-category, tier, channel, sub-channel, region, and account-class dimensions only; no brand, account, or wholesaler identifiers; all cells aggregate to N ≥ 10.

PPTX Studio ✨

supplier presentation generator · native PowerPoint export

What it is: A presentation studio that turns Hoodie analysis into a native, editable PowerPoint deck for supplier quarterly business reviews. A ribbon UI (Home / Insert / Transitions / Animations / Slideshow / Arrange) mirrors PowerPoint, with a slide rail, an editing canvas, and speaker notes.

Loop generation: Pick a loop dimension (e.g., category) and a set of values, and the studio builds one fully-formatted scorecard deck per value automatically — title, performance scorecards, channel and tier breakdowns, and talking points — from the live data.

Multiple decks: Work on several decks at once via the deck tabs across the top of the studio — click a tab to switch, double-click to rename, the × to close, and + Deck to start a new one. Each deck keeps its own loop dimension, slides, template, and preview value, so a category-loop deck and a supplier-loop deck can stay open side by side.

Dynamic variables (live tokens): Any slide text can embed bracket tokens that resolve per loop value at render and on export. The syntax is [token]. While editing text, type [ to open a live autocomplete (arrow keys to move, Enter or Tab to insert, Esc to dismiss) — the same idea as Snowflake's in-editor suggestions. Available tokens: [supplier] (the current loop value), [period], [rank], [peer_count], and the bound metrics [volume_growth], [revenue_growth], [pod_growth], [headroom_pt]. Tokens that don't resolve for the previewed value are highlighted so nothing ships blank.

Export: Produces a real .pptx with editable text, native charts, transitions, and entrance/exit animations (fade, appear, wipe exported exactly; fly/zoom/grow approximated as fade). Decks open and edit normally in PowerPoint or Google Slides.

Channels

Sub-channel-level intelligence across on-premise and off-premise channels

On-premise channel

sub-channel matrix · heatmap · trajectory · account class · new-item velocity

What it shows: The on-premise channel intelligence view. Aggregate channel scorecards at top (coverage, accounts under measurement, sub-channels tracked, history depth). Below: a 5-column sub-channel matrix showing R13 growth, velocity, premium index, and trend by venue type. Further sections include a sub-channel × category heatmap, longitudinal trajectory chart of 8 sub-channels (premium index over time), account-class concentration bars by sub-channel, and new-item velocity (days-to-100-accounts). At the top sits a "What's being poured right now" live-momentum board — the most recent four weeks of on-premise depletions ranked by current pour velocity at category × tier, with an accelerating/cooling delta vs the prior four weeks. It is the leading edge of the channel, surfacing momentum weeks before a quarterly read and at a granularity off-premise scanner data cannot reach.

How to read it: Hero scorecards establish scope. The matrix is the main read — each row is a sub-channel (Casino, Hotel, Country Club, Fine Dining, Casual Dining, Sports Bar, Bar/Lounge, Resort) with its R13 growth, average velocity, premium index, and a directional trend marker. The heatmap shows where each category is hottest across sub-channels. Trajectory chart shows premium index over time across the 8 sub-channels.

Controls: No view-level controls — driven by the global filter panel.

Customer use cases: Where are on-prem sub-channels accelerating? Where is premium index strongest? Which sub-channels have the longest new-item ramp-up time? Where is the long tail less developed (D-class concentration)? Which venues should the field team prioritize this quarter?

Off-premise channel

sub-channel matrix · heatmap · trajectory · account class · new-item velocity

What it shows: Mirror of the on-prem view for off-premise channels. Aggregate scorecards (coverage, accounts, sub-channels, history depth) plus matrix, heatmap, trajectory, account-class concentration, and new-item velocity across 8 off-prem sub-channels: Liquor Chain, Liquor Independent, Grocery, Mass Merchant, Warehouse Club, Drug, Convenience, Online/DTC. It also carries the off-premise comp to the on-prem live board — "What's going home right now" — ranking the most recent four weeks of take-home depletions by current sell-through. Read side-by-side with the on-premise board, it tells the two-basket story: the same consumer leans premium and experiential on-premise but take-home value and format (multi-serve RTD, mid-tier) off-premise.

How to read it: Same conventions as the on-prem view. Notable differences in off-prem patterns: account-class concentration is dramatically higher than on-prem — warehouse clubs are 88% A-class, online/DTC is 80% A-class. The heatmap substitutes Wine for Rum since wine is the dominant off-prem category. The trajectory chart Y-axis is calibrated to off-prem premium index ranges (55–150).

Controls: No view-level controls — driven by the global filter panel.

Customer use cases: Chain vs independent dynamics by category. Premium index trajectory by retail format. Where is innovation hitting fastest in retail? Which off-prem formats are picking up category share? What is the structural account-class concentration in each retail format?

Chain accounts

individual chains · distribution depth · authorization velocity · strategic quadrant

What it shows: An account-level view at chain granularity, designed for the chain-team workflow inside distributor commercial ops. Four hero scorecards (172 chains tracked, 73% avg distribution depth, 52-day median authorization velocity, 61% chain-driven share of channel volume). Below: chain landscape grid of 16 anonymized chain operators as profile cards; strategic quadrant plotting each chain by distribution depth × R12 growth; distribution depth ranking and new-item authorization velocity ranking; chain × category growth heatmap; and 6 chain-team-specific key insight callouts.

How to read it: The landscape grid is the orientation view — each card represents one anonymized chain operator with primary channel (left border color), premium-tier skew (badge), store count and geography, and four working metrics (R12 growth, velocity per door, distribution depth, authorization velocity). The strategic quadrant divides chains into four working categories: Anchor (high depth, high growth — protect), Expansion opportunity (low depth, high growth — push authorizations), Maturity (high depth, low growth — defend), and Watch (low depth, low growth — structural headwinds).

Methodology — anonymization: Chains are presented under stable cluster IDs (Chain A through Chain P). Cluster IDs rotate independently of brand-clustering IDs elsewhere in the platform — Chain A here is not Chain A in brand-clustering or anonymous position. Profile attributes (store count, geography, channel) are shown at sufficient granularity to be analytically useful without enabling unique identification of individual operators; combinations are vetted against the same N≥10 minimum that governs the rest of the platform.

Controls: Every visualization has a ⇄ Table flip. No view-level filters; driven by the global filter panel.

Customer use cases: Chain-team weekly planning and chain QBR prep. Distribution-depth gap analysis (where authorized SKUs are not yet carried in stores under the same banner). New-launch routing (which chains authorize fastest, which slowest, which by tier fit). Strategic quadrant input for chain-team budget allocation discussions. The view exists because chain teams are a structurally distinct customer inside distributor commercial ops, and rep-tier aggregation (small / regional / national) does not surface chain-specific workflow intelligence.

Position & comparison

How your wholesaler stands against the industry composite, by measure and by demographic

Wholesaler vs industry

measure-aware comparison · 14 measures · 7 report tables

What it shows: The wholesaler vs industry comparison view. Four hero stat cards at the top show your wholesaler's R13 base measures alongside the industry composite. Below the hero, seven comparison tables span top growers, bottom laggards, price tiers, on-prem sub-channels, census divisions, new item maturity cohorts, and account class concentration. Each row shows your value, the industry value, and the delta with a diverging bar.

How to read it: The measure dropdown is the most important control. It changes the underlying measure shown across all tables. The 14 available measures are grouped into Growth (volume_growth, revenue_growth, pod_growth, accounts_growth, acceleration), Share (volume_share, revenue_share, pod_share, accounts_share, activation, velocity), and Derived (price_mix, premium_idx, pod_efficiency). Index-type measures display on a 100-baseline integer scale; growth measures display as percentages.

Controls: Measure dropdown organized into three optgroups (Growth, Share, Derived). 14 selectable measures total.

Customer use cases: Where am I outperforming or under-indexing the industry on this specific measure? Where are my supplier QBR leverage points? Which census divisions am I winning and losing? What is the delta on each derived metric vs the industry composite?

Anonymous position

backbar & shelf placement

What it shows: Backbar (server-facing) and shelf (consumer-facing) placement across four price tiers and four spirits categories. Each bottle silhouette represents one share-of-distribution unit within a tier × category cell, grouped into anonymous clusters labeled A through W.

How to read it: Bottle height encodes the metric currently selected. Bottle color encodes the R12 growth bucket (dark green to dark coral). Cluster letters are abstract groupings, not brand identifiers. Backbar tiers run Prestige · Premium · Call · Well top-to-bottom; shelf tiers run Stretch · Eye level · Reach · Stoop.

Controls: Metric tabs at the top — Share · Velocity · Premium index · Composite. Selection applies to both grids simultaneously so backbar and shelf can be compared on the same metric.

Customer use cases: Where does the category have strong placement by tier and physical position? Where are the gaps in premium-tier placement? How do server-facing and consumer-facing distribution look on the same metric?

Profile shape

5-axis radar · derived metric fingerprint

What it shows: A radar chart visualizing all five derived metrics on one polygon — Velocity, Activation, Premium Index, Price/Mix, and POD Efficiency — each normalized 0–100. The shape of the polygon is the analytical fingerprint of the entity being plotted.

How to read it: Shape matters more than area. A polygon stretched toward one axis indicates strength in that dimension; a balanced polygon indicates evenness across metrics. Multiple polygons overlaid allow direct comparison — categories, sub-channels, price tiers, or census divisions plotted against one another. Filter modifiers (channel cut, region, period) reshape the polygon.

Controls: Compare dropdown (Categories, Sub-channels, Price tiers, Census divisions). Channel cut selector (All, On-prem all, On-prem sub-channels, Off-prem all). Region selector. Period selector (R12 vs prior R12, R3 vs prior R3, CYTD vs CYTDPY, CM vs CMPY).

Customer use cases: What does my book look like structurally? Where does each sub-channel or category over- or under-index across derived metrics? How does shape shift when channel or region filters are applied? Which categories are balanced contributors vs spiky single-metric drivers?

Demographics

buyer composition · cross-category overlap · cohort migration · placement gap

What it shows: An 11-section deep-dive into buyer demographics. Sections include: age cohort × category heatmap, gender split by sub-category, sub-channel buyer demographic profiles, income tier × premium aged spirits, demographic shift (median buyer age R3 vs trailing 3yr), cross-category buyer overlap, premium ladder progression with trade-up rates, birth-year cohort migration tracking, buyer economics by category (frequency, tenure, annual spend, repeat rate), the wholesaler's demographic placement gap analysis, and five Key Insight callouts.

How to read it: The page progresses from descriptive (who buys what) to behavioral (how do buyers move across categories) to predictive (cohort migration trajectories) to actionable (your specific demographic placement gap). The "Your demographic placement gap" section is the most directly actionable view — it compares your wholesaler's account-mix demographic skew against the category's actual buyer demographic, surfacing misalignment opportunities.

Controls: No view-level controls — driven by the global filter panel.

Methodology: Demographics are derived from consumer panel data with single-year-of-age recorded per panelist, combined with Hoodie depletion data for category context. Cohort tracking uses birth-year cohorts (not age ranges) so that the same set of panelists can be followed longitudinally. All cells reflect N≥100 observations; no individual consumer data is exposed.

Customer use cases: Supplier QBR data on buyer composition. Account-targeting refinement (placing categories where their actual buyers shop). Innovation evaluation against demographic backdrop. Detecting demographic-placement misalignment in your portfolio.

Portfolio analysis

Concentration risk, brand clustering, premiumization mix, and distribution quality

Anchor SKU dependency

top 10 concentration · Pareto risk

What it shows: The share of each category's sales captured by its top 10 brands ("anchor SKUs"), with the remaining brands grouped as the long tail. Four horizontal Pareto bars, one per spirits category, plus a 24-month trend line showing how concentration is changing.

How to read it: Each bar segment is sized to its share of the category. Dark navy segments are the top 5 brands (core anchors), teal segments are ranks 6–10 (secondary anchors), and gray is the long tail. The CR10 number on the right is the share of the category sitting in those top 10 brands. High CR10 = anchor-dependent (fragile if any anchor stumbles). Low CR10 = diversified (resilient). The trend chart shows whether concentration is tightening or loosening over the trailing 24 months.

Controls: Metric switcher — 9L volume share · revenue share · POD share. Volume share is the traditional concentration read. Revenue share usually shows tighter concentration in premium-skewed categories like tequila. POD share runs the highest because dominant brands have near-universal distribution.

Customer use cases: Which categories are most exposed to a single brand's stumble? Where is the long tail thick enough to support new brand entry? How is concentration moving — tightening (anchors gaining ground) or loosening (fragmentation, innovation, new entrants)? For a distributor: which categories require protection of anchor relationships vs. which permit portfolio diversification?

Brand clustering

distribution shape within a category

What it shows: Scatter plot of approximately 120 anonymous brand markers within one selected category. The X axis is a velocity index (0 to 100). The Y axis is R12 growth percentage (-22% to +28%). The cloud's shape is the analytical signal — concentration, gaps, and outliers communicate distribution structure that category averages hide.

How to read it: Each dot represents one brand as a non-identified marker. Dot color encodes the R12 growth bucket. The chart is divided into four labeled quadrants — winners (high velocity, high growth), risers (low velocity, high growth), laggards (low velocity, low growth), and declining leaders (high velocity, low growth). Look for cloud shapes — diffuse, bimodal, banded, clustered.

Controls: Category dropdown (Whiskey, Vodka, Tequila, Rum). Census Region. Census Division (cascading from region selection).

Customer use cases: Is category growth broad-based or driven by a small group of outliers? Where does the bulk of the population sit relative to the zero line? How does the population shape differ between regions?

Premiumization spread

volume share vs revenue share

What it shows: Scatter plot of anonymous brands within one category, plotting 9L volume share on the X axis against revenue share on the Y axis. A 45° dashed line marks the tier-neutral position where revenue share equals volume share.

How to read it: Above the line means premium-skewed (the brand earns more revenue share than volume share). Below the line means value-skewed. Dot color encodes deviation from the 45° line — teal above, coral below, neutral grey when close. Three view modes change what the chart draws.

Controls: Category, Census Region, and Census Division dropdowns. Three view-mode tabs: Current snapshot shows each brand's present position, 12-month trajectory draws arrows from each brand's prior position to its current one, 5-year category drift shows the category centroid migrating along the line.

Customer use cases: Where is premiumization actually happening at the brand level? Which brands are deflating? How has the overall category position shifted over five years?

Distribution quality

composite score + 24-month trajectory

What it shows: One composite distribution quality score per scope, with three time-period score cards (R12, YTD, CM) above a 24-month rolling trajectory chart. Score is defined as POD growth × velocity growth × price/mix growth blended into a single percentage.

How to read it: Each score card displays the period score and a delta versus the prior period — up triangle teal for positive delta, down triangle coral for negative. The line chart shows 24-month rolling trajectories with one line per category and a dashed grey line for the all-spirits aggregate.

Controls: Cascading Category / Census Region / Census Division dropdowns. Default view is all four categories displayed simultaneously.

Customer use cases: Single-number distribution health by category and geography. Which categories are improving versus eroding on the composite. Detection of inflection points before they appear in headline volume.

Growth dynamics

Growth and acceleration analysis across time, geography, and underlying drivers

Category growth and acceleration

paired bars + rolling lines

What it shows: Two paired sections. The top pair shows growth-rate bars by category with independent time framings on each side. The bottom pair shows rolling-line trajectories of growth rate over time, again with independent framings.

How to read it: Bars are colored by direction — teal for positive growth, coral for negative. The two bar panels can be set to different framings (R12, CYTD, R3, CM) so divergence between panels signals inflection. Lines are colored by category — amber whiskey, blue vodka, teal tequila, navy rum. Slope on the line charts encodes acceleration.

Controls: Four independent framing dropdowns. Bars accept R12 vs prior R12 · CYTD vs CYTDPY · R3 vs prior R3 · CM vs CMPY. Lines accept R12 rolling 12 months · R3 rolling 12 months · CM last 12 months · CQ last 8 quarters.

Customer use cases: Which categories are accelerating versus decelerating? Does current momentum diverge from the rolling-period view? How does the trajectory compare across time horizons?

Growth decomposition

PVM waterfall · POD × velocity × price/mix

What it shows: A waterfall decomposing revenue change into three mechanical drivers — POD (distribution), velocity (per-POD rate of sale), and price/mix (price-taking plus premiumization). Bars walk from the prior period's revenue to the current period's revenue, with each transition bar showing one driver's contribution. The chart forces the audience to read growth structurally rather than as a single headline number.

How to read it: Navy bars on either end are total revenue positions (starting and ending). Teal bars are positive contributions; coral bars are negative. The bar height represents the magnitude of the driver's effect in dollar terms. The connecting dashed lines show the floating baseline — where each bar starts equals where the previous bar ended. Two categories with identical headline growth can have entirely different driver profiles: one growing on POD expansion with declining velocity is healthier than one growing on price-taking alone.

Controls: Category dropdown (Whiskey, Vodka, Tequila, Rum, All spirits). Comparison period — R12 vs prior R12, YTD vs PYTD, CY vs PY, CM vs PM.

Customer use cases: Diagnose category health — is growth coming from distribution, demand, or price? Identify deceleration signals — which driver turned first? Compare categories with similar headline growth but different mechanics. Plan trade investment by driver — distribution programs target POD, depletion programs target velocity, brand programs target price/mix.

Geographic lead-lag

division-level trend timing

What it shows: A US heatmap rendered at account-level granularity, with census division boundaries drawn on top. The heat texture reflects sub-division concentration of lead-lag intensity (bourbon-belt density, urban-coastal clusters, etc.), but only the nine division-level scores are exposed numerically — the account-level texture is visible but not aggregable, which is the data-fiduciary posture made visual.

How to read it: Dark navy and sage areas are leader divisions — they tend to adopt trends first. Terracotta and rust shades are laggard divisions — they pick up trends 6 to 18+ months after leaders. Within each division, the heat texture shows where category intensity concentrates, but no sub-division score is reported. Each division shows its abbreviation and score (range -5 to +5). Strategic read: growth concentrated in leader divisions indicates the category has runway — the trend has not fully diffused yet. Growth concentrated in laggard divisions suggests the peak may be passing — early adopters have already moved on.

Controls: Category dropdown (Whiskey, Vodka, Tequila, Rum). Time period dropdown — CM (current month), PM (prior month), CY (current year), PY (prior year), YTD, PYTD. Switching periods reveals which divisions are accelerating their lead, which are decelerating, and which structural patterns have held stable across the time window.

Customer use cases: Distributor planning by territory — when should a division expect a category trend to arrive? Lifecycle diagnosis — is the category early, mid, or late in its diffusion across the country? Trajectory diagnosis — comparing CM and PYTD reveals which leaders are intensifying vs cooling. Allocation strategy — should resources go to leader divisions (early lift) or laggard divisions (sustained late-stage growth)?

Metric trajectories

component-level decomposition

What it shows: Five derived metrics (Velocity, Activation rate, Premium index, Price/mix growth, POD efficiency) stacked vertically. Each metric occupies its own section with paired panels — a current-period bar chart on the left and a 24-month rolling line chart on the right.

How to read it: Left bars give the current value of the metric across the four categories. Right lines show the metric's 24-month trajectory with one line per category. For centered metrics (Premium index, POD efficiency), bars show deviation from 1.0. For signed metrics (Price/mix growth), bars diverge from zero with teal positive and coral negative.

Controls: None at the section level. Filtering happens upstream in the Distribution quality view.

Customer use cases: When the composite distribution quality score moves, which component metric drove the move? Which derived metrics are converging or diverging across categories? Which trajectories are flattening or accelerating?

Platform & reference

Role-shaped views, governance and trust architecture, derived metrics reference, and filter utility

What your teams see

commercial VP desktop · sales rep mobile · role-shaped views

What it shows: Side-by-side mockups demonstrating how the platform extends across roles within the distributor organization. Left: Commercial VP desktop dashboard (the dashboard you're using). Right: sales rep mobile view showing an account-prioritized call list with acceleration alerts, watch list of declining accounts, and today's priority calls.

How to read it: The desktop mockup is a compressed rendering of the executive view — portfolio stats, sub-category performance, acceleration alerts. The phone mockup shows what a rep sees on the route: morning greeting, acceleration banner ("3 accounts hot this week"), today's priority calls with growth/risk badges, watch list of slipping accounts, and a bottom navigation. Same Hoodie data, same anonymization rules, different role-shaped views.

Controls: This is a positioning view; no controls.

Customer use cases: Demonstrate the role-extension capability of the platform to distributor leadership. Show how Hoodie intelligence reaches the rep working the route, not just the commercial leadership team. Position the platform as an organizational system rather than a single dashboard.

Data trust

anonymization architecture · fiduciary commitments

What it shows: Documentation of the platform's anonymization architecture and data fiduciary commitments. Six info sections cover: the data fiduciary positioning statement, what is never shown (brand names, account names, single-wholesaler-identifying data, sub-N=10 cells, time-stamped events), what is shown (categories, sub-categories, channels, sub-channels, tiers, account classes with N≥10, census divisions, time periods), the four-step anonymization data flow, cluster-rotation methodology (why Cluster A in one view is not the same brand as Cluster A in another view), and platform commitments.

How to read it: Each section uses red ✕ markers for protected layers and green ✓ markers for shown dimensions. The anonymization flow diagram shows enforcement at four points: raw data → aggregation engine → anonymization rules → display layer. Display-layer enforcement is the critical structural commitment — a brand name cannot reach the display even if earlier layers fail to strip it.

Controls: This is a policy view; no controls.

Customer use cases: Reference for distributor data committees evaluating the platform. Documentation of trust architecture for supplier conversations. The "data fiduciary" positioning made concrete and auditable, with explicit commitments listed for distributor accountability.

Governance

WSWA Data Committee · decision scope · distributor veto rights

What it shows: The WSWA Data Committee structure, decision scope, operating cadence, and "owner-operator" positioning. Documents the platform's governance as distributor-owned through WSWA, Hoodie-operated, with explicit veto rights for distributors on anonymization rule changes.

How to read it: The Data Committee has 7 distributor seats, 2 WSWA leadership seats, and 1 non-voting Hoodie operational seat. Quorum is 6 of 9; majority is 5 of 9. Any 3 distributor seats can veto changes to anonymization rules, data-sharing terms, or partner additions — regardless of overall majority. Decision scope explicitly covers product roadmap, anonymization changes, data partner approvals, output policy, strategic partnerships, and annual plan.

Controls: This is a policy view; no controls.

Customer use cases: Reference for distributor leadership on the governance structure. Explicit positioning that this platform extends SipSource (it does not replace VIP — that conversation is framed as a later step). The "owner-operators not customers" framing is the structural commitment that distinguishes this from a vendor relationship.

Derived metrics

framework reference

What it shows: Reference page for the five derived metrics. Each block presents the metric name, formula, brief description, and a four-category bar visualization of current values.

Formulas covered: Velocity = 9L ÷ Accounts Sold · Activation rate = Accounts Sold ÷ POD · Premium index = Revenue Share ÷ 9L Share · Price/mix growth = Revenue Growth − 9L Growth · POD efficiency = 9L Share ÷ POD Share

How to read it: Each metric has a description chip and a current-value bar across four categories. Ratio-based metrics (Premium index, POD efficiency) display bars as deviation from 1.0, with a vertical reference at the neutral position. Signed metrics (Price/mix growth) display bars diverging from zero with teal positive and coral negative.

Controls: None — this is a static reference.

Customer use cases: Definitions reference during a meeting. Common vocabulary for cross-team conversations. Quick check of current category values without filtering or interpretation.

Global filter panel

slide-out filter · global scope · per-view overrides

What it shows: A slide-out filter panel accessible via the "Filters" button in the top bar. The panel slides in from the right on click and offers two tabs — Product (Categories, Sub-categories, Price tiers, Aging tier, Format) and Market (Channels, On-prem sub-channels, Off-prem sub-channels, Account class, Census divisions). Each section is independently expandable and has its own internal search and per-option case-equivalent count.

How to read it: Global filters set baseline dimensions that apply across every view in the dashboard. Per-view filter controls (where present) override the global filter for that view. Counts displayed next to each filter option (e.g., "Tequila 28.7M") indicate the underlying volume that would be included by selecting that option. The filter panel deliberately excludes brand-level filtering, since brand-level resolution is prohibited by the anonymization architecture.

Controls: Click "Filters" in the top bar to open the panel. Click Apply to confirm selections (a green toast confirms application). Click Cancel, click outside the panel, or press Esc to close without applying. Click any section header to expand or collapse that section.

Customer use cases: Set a daily lens that applies across the whole dashboard (e.g., "Premium tier + On-Premise + South Atlantic"). Filter scope to specific product or market dimensions for analytical exploration. Refine views to a specific business segment for QBR prep or supplier conversations.
